common_name: Haut Black Raspberry (Late-Ripening Maryland-Bred Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring; Haut was released from the University of Maryland black raspberry breeding program in 1984 and ripens several days later than most blackcap cultivars, stretching the harvest window.

directions: Set out dormant canes or rooted tip layers in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants to allow good air movement between canes. Haut came out of the University of Maryland's black raspberry breeding program and was released in 1984, valued mainly for ripening about three to five days behind earlier standards like Bristol and Jewel, which lets a home planting spread its blackcap harvest over a longer stretch of summer rather than concentrating it into a single flush. Head back the tips of vigorous new primocanes in midsummer to force the lateral branches that will carry the following year's crop, and cut spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest to reduce disease carryover into the next season. Because black raspberries are prone to cane diseases in humid weather, favor an open, breezy planting site and avoid working around wet foliage.

common_name: Blackhawk Black Raspberry (Cold-Hardy Iowa State Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Blackhawk was released by Iowa State University in 1955 specifically for winter hardiness and anthracnose tolerance in the upper Midwest, and it is self-fertile.

directions: Plant dormant canes in full sun in well-drained soil, giving each hill enough room for air to move freely through the canes. Blackhawk was bred at Iowa State University and released in 1955 at a time when Midwest black raspberry plantings were routinely losing canes to hard winters and to anthracnose, a fungal cane disease that thrives in wet springs, and it remains one of the hardiest and most disease-tolerant blackcap cultivars available for northern gardens today. Plants are self-fertile and set a full crop from a single planting, producing medium to large glossy black fruit with good flavor on vigorous, upright canes. Tip-prune new primocanes in summer to promote branching, and remove old floricanes immediately after harvest to keep the planting open and reduce disease pressure through the following winter.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Mac Black Raspberry (Late-Season Michigan Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring on a trellis; Mac Black is a Michigan-origin selection of uncertain parentage that ripens roughly a week to ten days later than most black raspberries, extending the picking season into late summer.

directions: Plant dormant canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and train the tall, vigorous canes onto a trellis or wire support, since Mac Black grows noticeably taller and more upright than older black raspberry standards. Originating in Michigan from parentage that was never clearly recorded, Mac Black is prized chiefly for ripening about a week to ten days after most other blackcap cultivars have finished, giving gardeners who also grow an early type like Bristol or Jewel a meaningfully longer overall black raspberry season. The medium-to-large berries are firmer than many blackcaps, holding up well for fresh eating, freezing, or preserves, and the canes show useful field tolerance to anthracnose. Remove spent floricanes right after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per hill to keep the planting productive and easy to pick.

common_name: Vincent Kiwi (Low-Chill Fuzzy Kiwifruit for Warm Winters)

planting.note: Plant after last frost in full sun on a sturdy trellis; Vincent needs far fewer winter chill hours than Hayward, making it one of the better fuzzy kiwi choices for mild-winter Gulf Coast and Deep South gardens, but it is a female vine and still needs a male pollinizer nearby.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and train the vine onto a sturdy arbor or trellis capable of supporting many years of heavy growth. Vincent is a female fuzzy kiwi cultivar developed for areas with mild winters that do not reliably provide the roughly 800 chilling hours Hayward needs, which is why California Rare Fruit Growers lists it alongside Elmwood, Dexter, and Abbott as suitable options for southern California, the Gulf Coast, and Florida rather than the traditional cool-winter kiwi belt. Fruit is large and egg-shaped with good flavor, but because kiwi vines are dioecious, Vincent must be planted near a compatible male vine to set a crop, as it will not produce fruit on its own. Prune hard during dormancy to control the vine's naturally rampant growth and to keep fruiting wood within easy reach for harvest.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Abbott Kiwi (Low-Chill New Zealand Fuzzy Kiwifruit)

planting.note: Plant after last frost in full sun on a sturdy trellis; Abbott is one of the original New Zealand fuzzy kiwi selections and tolerates lower winter chill than Hayward, recommended for warm-winter regions including the Gulf Coast, but it is female and requires a male pollinizer vine nearby.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a strong permanent trellis or arbor since the vine becomes heavy and long-lived. Abbott is one of the early New Zealand fuzzy kiwi selections bred alongside Hayward and Allison in the twentieth century, and unlike Hayward it tolerates lower winter chill accumulation, which is why extension sources recommend it for warm-winter, low-chill regions such as southern California, the Gulf Coast, and Florida where Hayward struggles to break dormancy evenly. As a female-only cultivar it never sets fruit on its own and needs a male vine planted within pollinating distance during bloom. Prune annually while dormant to remove old fruiting wood and keep the vigorous canopy manageable, and mulch to conserve soil moisture through hot summers.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Allison Kiwi (New Zealand Fuzzy Kiwifruit Selection)

planting.note: Plant after last frost in full sun on a sturdy trellis; Allison is a female New Zealand fuzzy kiwi selection named for early nurseryman Alexander Allison, and it needs a male pollinizer vine, with growers often planting roughly one male for every eight female vines.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and give the vine a sturdy, permanent trellis, since fuzzy kiwi vines grow large and live for decades. Allison is one of the historic New Zealand fuzzy kiwi cultivars developed in the early twentieth century alongside Hayward, named for nurseryman Alexander Allison, and it remains a female-only selection that will not fruit without a nearby male vine, with a common pollination guideline of about one male for every eight to ten female vines. Fruit quality is good and comparable to other classic New Zealand selections, though Hayward remains the dominant commercial standard worldwide. Prune during winter dormancy to thin overcrowded canes and expose fruiting wood to light, and water deeply and regularly through the growing season since kiwi vines have relatively shallow roots and dislike drying out.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research
